Senses.Explanation: To take up and present means to hold something forth in active, public handling. Yuanwu Keqin gives the clearest boundary: agile response that shows three from one and weighs the occasion is what is called 提持; elsewhere he pairs it with carrying the school and taking up the ancestral seal. Feiyin Tongrong raises his staff while presenting one move face to face, Jiguang Huo takes up the authoritative command from the abbot's seat, and Baiyu Jingsi describes Mazu Daoyi's sickbed answer as an all-out presentation for others. An unnamed challenger can also appraise how an elder has handled the matter, while Gulin Qingmao preserves the underlying sense of personally taking up the staff and bowl. The verb therefore records enacted sustaining and presentation, not lineage succession alone.

Senses.Explanation: To bring something up and call attention to it: to prompt a person or repeatedly return a saying or matter to notice and examination. In a public exchange, an unnamed monk asks Gushan Shenyan to prompt him about the lineage matter; Gushan calls him closer and says, "This is prompting you." Hongzhi Zhengjue describes both participants in an exchange as each putting out a hand and bringing up the matter. Dahui Zonggao uses the verb both critically, for going once through an old saying and calling that freedom from words, and instructively, for bringing something up from time to time and amid walking, sitting, emotion, and responsive dealings. Wumen Huikai says many pick up Zhaozhou Congshen's answer and many bring it under examination. Foyan Qingyuan recalls receiving repeated earnest prompting from his late teacher. The Zen bend is the interpersonal and case-facing use: this ordinary act of calling attention becomes something done in the interview, received by Foyan Qingyuan from his late teacher, or repeatedly directed at a recorded saying, without naming a separate regimen.

Senses.Explanation: Lifting a physical object and taking up a saying are distinct attested acts: hands raise staffs or whisks, while speech raises a case, word, or question. To lift, pick up, or hold aloft a physical object, with this concrete action repeatedly made into a visible move in public encounters. Shengguang holds up a whisk and asks what it is called. An unnamed newcomer lifts a sitting cloth and makes a circle. Nanquan Puyuan lifts the disputed cat and asks the assembly to speak. Deng Yinfeng lifts his rosary when asked his age, and an unnamed Chan visitor lifts a tea bowl when asked about ‘the other side.’ These constructions move an object bodily into view; they are distinct from instructions to take up and sustain a verbal question before attention.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names to take up a saying or question for sustained attention, not to lift or hold up a physical object. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. To take up a saying or question and keep it actively before attention. Zhongfeng Mingben repeatedly directs an assembly to do this with verbal objects: a saying without the flavor of meaning, one's assigned saying of inquiry, and the complete question ‘The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?’ His surrounding predicates require beginning with it, not moving from it, continuing forward with it, and sustaining questioning while walking or sitting. Dufeng Shan likewise instructs listeners to take up the saying they investigate at all times. This is not bodily lifting of an object; it is the continued taking-up of a verbal subject.

Senses.Note: The Huangbo newcomer, Fenyang, Deshan, and Tianyin passages are separate encounters rather than recensions of one inherited scene.

Senses.Explanation: 提起坐具 means “lift the sitting cloth.” An unnamed newcomer does it before Huangbo Xiyun, Fenyang Shanzhao and Deshan Xuanjian do it in separate encounters, and Tianyin Yuanxiu gives it as an instruction. The phrase can therefore report the gesture or command it.

Senses.Note: Incidental handling while travelling, leaning, retrieving, or describing an object does not establish this sense; each token still requires its complete action and speech frame.

Senses.Explanation: In formal hall speech, the phrase marks the deliberate gesture of lifting or holding up the staff to present it to the assembly. The retained Baoning address moves from a verse-like challenge to the explicit gesture and then the terse words “Careful, careful.” This supports a recurring demonstrative hall use, not a claim that every physical lifting of a staff is lexical.
